run.question: We're getting mapping errors and slow indexing on our events index. Can you check the field mappings for our app-188-index-* indexes and tell me if any have an unusually high number of fields? What's the exact field count for each?

report.summary: Only one of the four app-188-index-* indices has an unusually high field count: app-188-index-x with 523 top-level mapped fields (655 mapped fields counting its 132 keyword multi-field subfields), against exactly 10 top-level fields in each of app-188-index-a, -b and -c. The extra fields in app-188-index-x are generated, sequence-numbered names (counter_*, flag_*, label_*, metric_* stepping by 4, up to counter_0517) plus @timestamp and user_id, and the single document stored in that index carries exactly that style of field names, which is consistent with a dynamic-mapping field explosion — a hypothesis, not a proven creation mechanism. I could not observe the reported mapping errors or indexing slowness at all: this Run exposes only search/mappings/indices reads of the Elasticsearch target, with no server, ingest or deprecation logs, no index settings or templates, and the Prometheus probe for Elasticsearch indexing metrics returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE. So the field-count difference is established; the causal link to the errors is not.

claims.text: Four indices match app-188-index-*: app-188-index-a, app-188-index-b and app-188-index-c each have 0 documents and 227b store size (health green, status open), and app-188-index-x has 1 document and 204.4kb store size (health green, status open). These four are also the only indices in the entire target.

app-188-index-a has exactly 10 top-level mapped fields: @timestamp, action, duration_ms, error_message, event_type, ip_address, metadata, session_id, status, user_id (10 mapped fields in total including nested, 0 multi-field subfields, 1 text field).

app-188-index-b has exactly 10 top-level mapped fields with the same names as app-188-index-a (@timestamp, action, duration_ms, error_message, event_type, ip_address, metadata, session_id, status, user_id); 10 mapped fields in total, 0 multi-field subfields, 1 text field.
app-188-index-c has exactly 10 top-level mapped fields with the same names as app-188-index-a and -b; 10 mapped fields in total, 0 multi-field subfields, 1 text field.

app-188-index-x has 523 top-level mapped fields and 655 mapped fields counting nested definitions; the difference is exactly its 132 text fields that each carry a keyword multi-field (subfield_total 132, 132 text fields with subfields).

The field names in app-188-index-x are generated sequence-numbered names: 130 fields prefixed counter_ (highest counter_0517), plus flag_*, label_* and metric_* families stepping by 4, alongside only @timestamp, event_type and user_id as conventional names; field types are boolean 130, date 1, float 129, long 131, text 132.

The single document in app-188-index-x (@timestamp 2026-11-21T05:06:00Z, event_type user_action, user_id usr_12345, _id mfiA_KEBFz7Q4KB3WUiJ) carries the same generated names, e.g. counter_0517=517, flag_0002=true, label_0003="value_3", metric_0000=0.

app-188-index-x's mapping contains no object-typed fields with sub-properties (count_of_object_fields 0), so its 655 mapped fields are flat leaf fields plus keyword subfields rather than nested objects; the mapping's dynamic setting is not set on the index mapping (value null).

app-188-index-a, -b and -c do not show a high field count: each is 10 top-level fields and 10 mapped fields in total with no multi-field subfields, so a high field count is not a property of the app-188-index-* family as a whole and applies only to app-188-index-x.

The 523-field mapping of app-188-index-x appears to be a dynamic-mapping field explosion driven by a writer that emits per-event generated key names (counter_NNNN / flag_NNNN / label_NNNN / metric_NNNN), which is consistent with the one stored document carrying those keys; such growth would raise per-document field count and mapping size, plausibly contributing to slow indexing and to mapper_parsing_exception-style errors, but the creation mechanism was not observed in this Run.

A second candidate cause of mapping errors that the evidence cannot exclude is a type or field-name conflict between documents routed to the app-188-index-* pattern: app-188-index-a/-b/-c share a 10-field schema (including error_message, status, metadata, duration_ms) that app-188-index-x does not have, so a document written under a shared pattern/alias could hit conflicting mappings; nothing in the evidence shows such a rejected document.

The hypothesis that a high field count is present across the app-188-index-* family, or that app-188-index-a/-b/-c are mapping-bloated, is rejected: each of a, b and c has exactly 10 top-level mapped fields and 10 mapped fields in total.

Treat app-188-index-x as the index to fix: enumerate the counter_/flag_/label_/metric_ key generator on the writing side and flatten or map those keys explicitly (e.g. a fixed schema, or a field-name pattern routed to a long/keyword sub-field) instead of letting each event create new top-level field names, and reindex/rebuild app-188-index-x with the reduced schema if it keeps churning.

Before changing the schema, confirm the reported failure mode from Elasticsearch itself: read index settings and templates for app-188-index-* (especially index.mapping.total_fields.limit, dynamic templates and any alias/pattern routing shared with a/b/c) and the Elasticsearch server/ingest logs for mapper_parsing_exception or illegal_argument_exception messages naming these indices, none of which this Run could read.

gaps: No Elasticsearch server, ingest-pipeline or deprecation logs are available in this Run (only elasticsearch_list_indices, elasticsearch_mappings and elasticsearch_search), so the reported mapping errors were not observed; no mapper_parsing_exception message is in evidence.

Index settings and index templates could not be read, so index.mapping.total_fields.limit for app-188-index-x, any dynamic templates, and whether a/b/c/x share an alias or template are unknown; the observed 655 total mapped fields in app-188-index-x could therefore not be compared against the configured field limit, and a field-limit breach is not established.

No indexing-rate, indexing-latency or merge metrics for this Elasticsearch target are available; the discovery query {__name__=~"elasticsearch.*|es_indexing.*|.*indexing.*"} against Prometheus returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so slow indexing is unchecked rather than zero or absent.

There is no change_history integration in this Run, so when the 523-field mapping of app-188-index-x was created, and what changed it, is unknown; all mapping observations are the state at query time (2026-11-21T05:07Z) and cannot prove the mapping during the incident window.

The writer of app-188-index-* is not identifiable from the evidence: the only Kubernetes workloads present are kube-system, local-path-storage and otel-demo (22 pods), and no pod carries app-188 in its name, so the source of the generated counter_/flag_/label_/metric_ fields is unknown.
Only 1 document exists in app-188-index-x, so per-document field counts, rejected documents, and the distribution of field names across documents could not be sampled beyond that one document.
next_steps: Provide Elasticsearch server/ingest logs (or the exact error text of the mapping errors) filtered to app-188-index-*, so the failure mode can be attributed to a specific reason rather than inferred from field counts.
Retrieve GET app-188-index-x/_settings and _template/_index_template for app-188-index-* to see index.mapping.total_fields.limit, dynamic templates and any shared alias used by the four indices.
Identify the application that writes app-188-index-* documents and inspect its key-generation code for the counter_NNNN/flag_NNNN/label_NNNN/metric_NNNN naming.
